articles.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
articles.snippet: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
articles.full_text:
US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
- Published
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.
The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".
He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base".
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.
However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.
"The key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods... are also not subject to these new tariffs."
The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
- Published22 August

articles.title: Images of asteroid targeted to test Earth's defences reveal stadium-sized crater
articles.snippet: The asteroid's surface was transformed after a spacecraft was deliberately crashed into it four years ago
articles.full_text:
Images of asteroid targeted to test Earth's defences reveal stadium-sized crater
- Published
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.
The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.
"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."
The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
A key objective of the Hera mission is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, in order to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Hera's arrival on the scene is helping scientists answer many more questions too.
Not only did the collision alter the shape of Dimorphos, it also changed the way it moves.
"Before the Dart impact, Dimorphos was more like our own Moon - so it was always showing the same face to Didymos, and it was behaving quite nicely," explained Raducan.
"Now it's very, very chaotic - it's tumbling. Imagine a barrel that you throw down the stairs, and the barrel is rolling and it's moving, and basically that's what Dimorphos does right now around Didymos."
Hera has also taken detailed images of Didymos, revealing its surface in detail.
"The gravity at the surface of Didymos is about 40,000 times less than the gravity on Earth," said Naomi Murdoch, who is on the Hera mission team.
"We can already see some fascinating and complex geology. We can see regions of boulders.
"The smallest details that we can make out in these images are about 3m in size. So that means that all the boulders that you can see with your eyes are at least 3m big, and some as big as 10m. So what we're seeing here is boulders the size of cars and buses sitting on a world with almost no gravity."
The Hera mission will spend the next six months studying Dimorphos and Didymos, sending back more images taken from closer up in higher resolution.
"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.
The spacecraft is packed with instruments and also has two shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.
But the first images taken by Hera have also revealed a new challenge. Dimorphos and Didymos are travelling through space surrounded by hundreds of boulders ranging in size from tens of centimetres to metre-size rocks.
This will make it especially challenging to operate the spacecraft and cube satellites through this boulder field.
Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.
The biggest, which measures more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.
"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who has worked on both the Dart and Hera missions.
"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."
She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.
"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.
"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."
Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.
A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids - a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.
There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.
Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.
But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.
This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.
Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

articles.title: Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
articles.snippet: The Israeli PM says his trial should end after judges said there was little chance of conviction in one of three cases.
articles.full_text:
Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
- Published
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.
The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.
The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.
In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.
"The chances of conviction are low â to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.
The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case â concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 â met the threshold for criminality.
While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.
Netanyahu: What are the corruption charges?
- Published22 May 2020
However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.
It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.
He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.
The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.
The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.
For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.
This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.
While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.
Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

articles.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
articles.snippet: All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.
articles.full_text:
US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
- Published
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.
The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down. The tech-dominated Nasdaq has shed over 2%.
The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta were also down.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.
The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, but share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
- Published1 day ago
Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.
"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.
Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by more than 5%.
The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

articles.title: My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated
articles.snippet: BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in the war.
articles.full_text:
My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated
- Published
I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.
The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.
I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.
"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.
It turned my world upside down.
Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.
We stopped speaking.
Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.
Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.
After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.
Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground, external.
I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.
But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.
I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.
I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.
Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.
This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.
In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.
Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.
It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.
"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.
With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.
"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here
Watch our YouTube documentary here, external
As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.
Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.
I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.
She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.
At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."
She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.
"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.
She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.
The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.
She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.
With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.
Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.
Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.
"If they had seen me they would have killed me too."
Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.
"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.
Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.
The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.
These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.
The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.
The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.
Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.
He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.
As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.
I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.
I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.
He said he did not know anything about who killed them.
"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.
I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.
My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.
I turned to the Ukrainian military.
A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.
Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.
We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.
It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.
We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.
The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.
However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.
Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.
There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.
Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.
She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place
At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.
"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.
"Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

articles.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
articles.snippet: Despite widespread concern from residents ahead of the blast, officials say that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
articles.full_text:
US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
- Published
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked widespread fears of health and environmental problems across the region.
Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".
President Donald Trump said reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".
Plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused multiple times before Wednesday's detonation following public outcry and legal challenges.
Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.
"We are watching EPA's [Environmental Protection Agency] MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," he added.
The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.
No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" and "vindicated" after the detonation.
He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.
"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.
Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.
The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.
"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.
"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."
Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.
"I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.
Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"
But there is also caution from some.
Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".
Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".
Cameron Hamilton, administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.
In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.
It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.
The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.
But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.
Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

articles.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
articles.snippet: Swiss officials said relations would be kept through North Korea's embassy in Bern, and its own embassy in Beijing.
articles.full_text:
North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
- Published
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close amid a row over sanctions.
It said the move was in response to Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp. State media described this as "a blatant hostile act".
That camp is at the centre of claims that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
North Korea's foreign ministry said "any act of violating the sovereign rights" of the country and the interests of its citizens "can never be welcomed".
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.
Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.
The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.
Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997.
Switzerland's federal department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".
It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."
Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.
In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

articles.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
articles.snippet: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.
articles.full_text:
Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
- Published
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
How we came to a figure near half a million
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian â unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.

articles.title: Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Disruptions at Yemen's largest seaport could exacerbate hardships for millions of Yemenis, aid experts warn.
articles.full_text:
Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
The Houthi-held seaport is a critical lifeline for millions of Yemenis but has taken significant damage over the course of recent conflicts.
The Saudi-led coalition has launched renewed attacks on Houthi targets at Yemen’s port of Hodeidah as the armed group fights Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The strikes come amid significant Houthi territorial gains in recent weeks and escalating attacks by the group on Saudi Arabia.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Saudi coalition hits 60 Houthi military sites; Taiz sees ‘fierce battles’
- list 2 of 3Saudi coalition and Houthis exchange threats to bomb key ports
- list 3 of 3Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi attacks after Hodeidah strike
Hodeidah, which has repeatedly been attacked over the past decade, is critical to both Yemen’s economy and the supply of essential goods to millions of people in Houthi-controlled areas.
Here’s what we know:
How important is the port of Hodeidah?
The port of Hodeidah, situated on Yemen’s western Red Sea coast, is the country’s principal commercial seaport and has been under Houthi control since 2014.
It serves as a major entry point for food, fuel and other commercial goods as well as humanitarian assistance, supplying the densely populated northern and western regions of Yemen, including the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.
The port had eight berths and the capacity to accommodate 6,500 standard shipping containers in 2023. However, attrition due to Yemen’s more than a decade of conflict has reduced the number of operational berths and damaged cranes and storage facilities.
Despite this, in September 2025, the United Nations Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement estimated that the port handled about 70 percent of commercial imports and 80 percent of humanitarian aid coming into Yemen, calling it a “lifeline”.
“The closure or disruption [of the port] under the current circumstances would delay the arrival of food, medicine and fuel; increase transport costs and prices; and exacerbate the suffering of families already facing an acute humanitarian crisis,” said Abdusattor Esoev, Yemen Chief of Mission for the International Organization for Migration.
“At a time when millions of people in Yemen depend on humanitarian assistance and face severe food insecurity, Hodeidah remains a critical lifeline. The port is essential for bringing in food, fuel, medicines and other basic goods needed by civilians across northern Yemen,” said Francesca Quinto, the programme manager for Yemen for Doctors Without Borders.
However, the Houthis have long been accused of using Hodeidah’s port for both civilian and military purposes. Investigations have found that the group exploits commercial port facilities to smuggle in weapons from Iran, its chief ally.
“The ports of Hodeidah are key to commercial flows. However, the Houthis’ increasing militarisation of vital civilian infrastructure by smuggling and storing arms, fuel and narcotics is undermining the humanitarian functions they serve in wartime,” Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera.
Tawfiq al-Hamidi, a Yemeni lawyer and human rights activist, told Al Jazeera that the port has been misused by the group for smuggling despite its importance for Yemen’s population.
“Nevertheless, efforts must be made to protect the port as a civilian facility, and the Houthi movement must provide genuine guarantees,” he said.
Has the port been attacked before?
Yes. Since the start of Yemen’s civil war in September 2014, the port and its surrounding area have repeatedly come under attack from the Saudi-led coalition, the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. Pro-Yemeni government forces also tried to capture it in a 2018 offensive.
About 70 percent of Yemenis live in Houthi-controlled areas in the country’s west, where most goods arrive from the rest of the world through Red Sea ports. Humanitarian aid continues to enter through other ports, including Mocha and a major government-held port in Aden, but renewed fighting has made the overland flow of this aid to the country’s interior difficult. Humanitarian operations in Houthi-controlled areas have also been severely curtailed because of the detention of UN staff by the group.
In March 2015, shortly after launching its military intervention in support of the Yemeni government, the Saudi-led coalition began a partial maritime blockade on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.
A UN-brokered nationwide truce in April 2022 led to an easing of restrictions on fuel imports through Hodeidah. Further restrictions on commercial imports were lifted in early 2023, which also helped to revitalise the port.
But that recovery was then jeopardised by a campaign of US, British and Israeli strikes on Houthi-controlled areas beginning in 2024 and lasting into the next year, in retaliation for Houthi drone and missile attacks on Israel and Red Sea shipping, carried out ostensibly in the name of supporting Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave.
Why is Saudi Arabia attacking the port now?
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announced on Wednesday that it had launched new strikes against the Houthis at the port, days after it warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Houthis have promised not to let strikes against the port go unanswered.
Since the return of full-scale war to Yemen in September, the Houthis have made sweeping territorial gains across Yemen, pushing back the forces of the internationally recognised government.
A government counteroffensive launched in early October has failed to stem Houthi advances despite heavy air support. Government forces are now scrambling to defend Aden, the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“Broadly speaking, the strikes [on Hodeidah’s port] were a response to the shift on the battlefield in favour of the Houthis,” Ali al-Dhahab, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, told Al Jazeera.”
“They were aimed at undermining and crippling their economic and logistical capabilities, including infrastructure, such as ports and airports, as well as their military capabilities,” he said.
Escalating Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia targeting airports, oil infrastructure and commercial buildings also played a role in the decision, al-Dhahab said, mentioning Thursday’s attack on the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in Riyadh.
The following day, the Saudi-led coalition urged civilians near Hodeidah’s port to evacuate without providing specifics.
What could happen next?
Before Wednesday’s strikes, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree reiterated a threat of retaliation on Saudi seaports on the Red Sea, naming Jeddah’s port in particular.
Nabil Al-Bukairi, a Yemeni researcher and policy expert, told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia’s strikes on the port should not be taken as a warning. “I believe the strikes have gone beyond being merely symbolic,” he said.
“Continued bombardment would inevitably lead to its closure and render it inoperable once its infrastructure and logistical capabilities have been targeted,” he warned.
Even without a closure, strikes that disrupt the operations of the facility risk delays of critical aid as Yemen’s war shows no sign of an imminent end.

Experts say the move is a ‘logical response’ if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat.
Britain’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it takes “the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously,” after media outlets reported the Royal Air Force (RAF) had taken new precautions against possible drone attacks.
The Times and Sky News reported on Wednesday that planes would be moved to hangars and hardened shelters overnight, and anti-drone nets would be installed to protect any warplanes that remained exposed.

The MoD did not confirm the reports, but in a statement said it was “always adapting to counter any potential threats”.
Justin Bronk, a senior researcher at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank in London, told Al Jazeera that the RAF’s reported tactics would be “a sensible, logical response if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat”.
“The main bases used for RAF fighters, Coningsby, Marham and Lossiemouth all still have hardened aircraft shelters from the Cold War era that have been maintained in usable condition for both aircraft storage, protection and limited maintenance work,” Bronk said.
However, Bronk cautioned that there were not enough hardened shelters to protect all of the jets at each airbase, after squadrons were consolidated into ‘super bases’ following the end of the Cold War, and a “mistaken assumption” that such protection was no longer important.
The MoD said it was investing an additional 470 million pounds ($615m) “to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities”, and that 15 million pounds ($19.6m) had already been invested “in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites”.
Attack readiness
British authorities have regularly issued warnings about threats posed by Russia and Iran, and the government has urged the country to be prepared for different contingencies. In a report in October, members of Parliament warned that Britain’s military needed to make “dramatic progress” to be ready for a potential attack by Russia on a NATO country.
On Tuesday, Britain’s domestic MI5 intelligence service and the MoD issued a joint alert warning UK military suppliers to Ukraine about increasing sabotage attempts by Russia.
“Aircraft inside a standard hangar or a hardened aircraft shelter are protected from attacks by infiltrated adversary cells or terrorists with small drones,” explained RUSI’s Justin Bronk. “But only those in hardened shelters are protected from larger one-way attack drones like the Geran 2/3/4 series during a hypothetical wartime attack,” he added, referring to the Geran drones manufactured and operated by Russia, based on an original Iranian design.
Bronk said that even though hardened aircraft shelters seem old-fashioned, they are a “relatively low-risk, inexpensive and effective way to improve fighter fleet resilience in wartime.”
“They provide almost total protection from drones due to thick concrete and blast doors, and also mean that any unintercepted cruise missile can only destroy a single jet at most with a direct hit.”
US withdraws military aircraft
Earlier this month US forces responded to possible unauthorised drone activity over a military base in the United Kingdom, hosting American warplanes.
“No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected” at the eastern RAF Lakenheath base, a US Air Force spokesperson said in a statement at the time.
There was also an Iran-linked security scare on September 27 at the southwestern RAF Fairford base, which was used by the US planes. A group of men allegedly drove three vans up to a village near the site and abandoned them with filled petrol barrels inside, sparking a bomb scare and evacuation.
Washington had used the airbase in its war on Iran, and days after the September incident withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base. Two men have since been charged in a UK court over the incident, and three in the United States.
The US military also withdrew its planes from RAF Mildenhall, near Lakenheath, on November 9 , following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal and The Financial Times.

articles.title: World reacts to Trump’s new tariffs as US stocks tumble

articles.snippet: The new levies come after an eight-month investigation launched by the United States Trade Representative.
articles.full_text:
World reacts to Trump’s new tariffs as US stocks tumble
The new levies come after an eight-month investigation launched by the United States Trade Representative.
The Trump administration has announced new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union, claiming that excess production has given them an unfair advantage.
The proposed levies come after a months-long investigation into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan, launched after the Supreme Court struck down United States President Donald Trump’s sweeping global tariffs in February.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 4China Southern Airlines unit to buy 50 Boeing 737-8 planes
- list 3 of 4How close should Britain get to the EU?
- list 4 of 4Trump announces new trade tariffs: Which countries are affected?
The highest tariff rate announced on Wednesday would hit China the hardest, at 20 percent, adding to the roughly 25 percent duties that Trump imposed on China during his first term.
The proposed tariffs would not apply to about $30bn of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.
Washington has long accused China of subsidising its industries and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products, allegations that Beijing has once again denied.
“The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, urging the world’s two top economies to maintain stable relations.
Other US trading partners facing proposed new tariffs include India, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
Mexico and Norway were also part of the probe but were excluded from the new round of tariffs because investigations into their trade practices are still ongoing.
‘Cynical’ use of Section 301
The tariff announcement follows an eight-month investigation initiated by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.
“The administration’s use of Section 301 is cynical,” Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Al Jazeera. “It launched these investigations in order to support the president’s aim to set tariffs globally and to modify them at any time at the president’s will, and thus strip Congress of the authority to set tariff rates under the taxing power set forth in the Constitution.”
In a separate announcement, the White House also announced a proposed 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer, whose jets are widely used by US regional carriers operating under brands including United Express, Delta Connection and American Eagle. Finished aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-biggest export to the US.
The US also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices, according to a senior US official.
Global reaction
Several governments have reacted to the new tariff announcement, as has the European Union.
“The EU takes note of the publication by the US of preliminary findings pursuant to its Section 301 investigation concerning structural excess capacity in manufacturing sectors,” European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told Al Jazeera.
“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Gill added.
The Swiss government has also reacted, saying that it rejects the allegations stemming from the investigations.
“The timing right before the G20 [in mid-December] sets up those meetings as an opportunity for negotiation and increases risk of both inflationary pressures and macro volatility in 2027, reducing some of the benefit from easing gas prices,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
Norway has praised the decision.
“We have been clear throughout the process that Norway does not have policies that contribute to overcapacity. Norwegian companies produce in response to market demand,” Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said.
Markets react
US markets are trending down on news of the new tariffs. The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled 3.9 percent in early trading on Wednesday. The S&P 500 is down 2.8 percent, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slumped by 1.4 percent.
The price of gold – which is considered a safe investment in times of economic uncertainty – fell by more than 3 percent to its lowest level in more than a year. However, in addition to tariffs, the price was influenced by inflation data released on Wednesday which showed a 0.3 percent rise in one of the US Federal Reserve’s key metrics for assessing the rate of inflation. Higher inflation increases the chances of a rise in interest rates, which in turn weighs on the metal.
Bond yields in both the US and Europe dropped on Wednesday.
Germany’s 10-year bond yield, which is the benchmark for the eurozone, slid by 4.5 basis points to 3.2 percent, while the US 10-year Treasury note yield stumbled by 6.8 basis points to 4.834 percent, putting it on pace for its seventh daily drop over the past eight sessions.

articles.title: Estimates of Russians killed in Ukraine surpass all combined US war deaths since WWI
articles.snippet: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale war against the nation nearly five years ago.
articles.full_text:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale war against the nation nearly five years ago, according to an updated estimate released on Monday.
Based on analysis of leaked official data by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers from Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat, two Russian opposition outlets, Mediazona and Meduza, have confirmed that, accounting for time lags and troops reported missing in action, Russian fatalities jumped from 490,000 at the end of September to more than 720,000 since the start of the conflict in February 2022.
That number, CNN reports, equates to roughly one death every four minutes. The estimate does not include the number of soldiers wounded.
“We are confident that this data is authentic: it is verified against the list of names of the deceased (including records not yet published), the Register of Inheritance Cases, other leaked records from civil registry offices, the texts of court decisions from open sources, and previously published data from Rosstat itself,” Meduza reported.
The Kremlin has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early start of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu acknowledged that it stood at nearly 6,000. This has left many Russian civilians with perhaps little understanding of the full breadth of the conflict as President Vladimir Putin continues to suppress critical information regarding the war at home.
This grim assessment is particularly stark when placed next to U.S. military casualties. If accurate, the number of Russians dead in Ukraine has surpassed all combined U.S. military deaths since World War I.
According to official DoD numbers — exact death counts vary, with historians often clashing over official counts for years, even decades — the U.S. suffered 116,516 total military deaths in WWI; 405,399 military deaths in WWII; 36,574 military deaths during the Korean War; 58,220 during the Vietnam War; 382 in the Persian Gulf War; 2,459 in Afghanistan; 4,493 in Iraq; and 362 military deaths from conflicts in Grenada, Panama, Somalia and Beirut.
The total, 624,547, spanning over 100 years, still falls far below that of Russia in the past five.
While 700,000 lives lost is staggering, it still pales when compared to Soviet dead after Nazi Germany launched Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. During four years of war, it is estimated that 8.8 million to 10.7 million Soviet soldiers were killed. Combined with civilian deaths, that estimate hovers around the grim figure of 24 million Soviet deaths.

articles.snippet: The Pentagon announced a $2.82 billion Boeing contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, the final production lot under the program's original 2011 contract.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon on Tuesday announced a $2.82 billion Boeing contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, the final production lot under the program’s original 2011 contract.
The deal comes in about $350 million above the previous 15-tanker lot, which the Air Force bought for $2.47 billion a year ago. The earlier lot is expected to be complete by mid-2029 and the new lot by mid-2030, according to the Pentagon.
The Air Force has received 116 KC-46As so far, and 203 are on contract or in service worldwide, Boeing said. Japan and Israel also fly the tanker.
“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” Jake Kwasnik, KC-46 program vice president, said in Boeing’s release. “The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”
Tuesday’s award is the last of 13 production lots priced into the original contract, Boeing’s filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission show.
After that, the Air Force plans to buy up to 75 more KC-46As from Boeing through a program called Tanker Production Extension, according to an April contracting notice. The service wants 263 KC-46As for itself, which it says will fully replace its KC-135s, built in the 1950s and early 1960s.
Air Force Vice Chief of Staff Gen. John Lamontagne said the 75-jet buy depends on Boeing fixing some of the tanker’s problems, Reuters reported. He didn’t specifically identify the problems, but the best-known KC-46A issues involve the refueling boom and the Remote Vision System, or RVS, the cameras boom operators use to guide it.
“We are working through a couple of issues with the contractor, and we are not going to get a new contract for another 75 KC-46s until we work through some of those deficiencies,” Lamontagne told a Senate Armed Services subcommittee March 4. He said a decision was likely two years away.
Boeing said in June it had completed the first phase of flight testing on a redesigned RVS 2.0. The Air Force has projected fielding the upgraded system in summer 2027, three years later than originally planned.
The KC-46 program has been costly for Boeing. It built the tanker under a firm-fixed-price contract, which leaves the company to cover cost overruns, and has recorded more than $7 billion in losses, including $565 million late last year that Boeing blamed on higher production costs.
The service has said the main issues keeping KC-46s from being ready to fly are the reliability of the aerial refueling system and parts shortages. In May, the Air Force and Boeing agreed on a plan that, along with funding in the fiscal 2027 budget request, is expected to increase KC-46 availability by more than 20% by 2030.

articles.title: Japan to use Indian ranges for long-range missile training under new pact
articles.snippet: Japanese officials visited India in October to assess whether its missile ranges could accommodate training with anti-ship missiles and smaller attack drones.
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI — India will allow Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at its firing ranges for the first time as Tokyo looks overseas for facilities to test its long-range missile capabilities including surface-to-ship missiles.
The signing of a Letter of Intent (LOI) regarding the use of the Indian ranges was announced on Nov. 19, following a meeting between the two countries’ foreign and defense ministers in Tokyo.
The move marks a significant step in deepening defense cooperation between the two Asian countries.
Japanese officials visited India in October to assess whether its missile ranges could accommodate training with anti-ship missiles and smaller attack drones.
Chief of Staff of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force Masayoshi Arai told reporters in Tokyo last month that the visit’s aim was to determine how to conduct training that makes full use of the roughly 1,000-kilometer range of Japan’s Type-25 surface-to-ship missile, which he described as “a major challenge.”
Limited space in the island country for long-range live-fire exercises has prompted officials to look for training options overseas. Access to Indian ranges could help overcome that limitation.
To bolster its military strength amid growing concerns over China’s military activity in the region, Japan began deploying long-range missiles on the southern island of Kyushu this year. The deployment is part of Japan’s effort to strengthen its deterrence and stand-off defense capabilities as it makes a significant shift in its post-World War II security posture.
A joint statement by the two countries after last week’s meeting welcomed the signing of the Letter of Intent, “whereby Japan Self-Defense Forces would, for the first time, conduct live-fire training etc., including those involving surface-to-ship missiles, at firing ranges in India.”
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the arrangement was significant not only for expanding the scope of training for Japanese forces but also as a demonstration of a new phase in Japan-India cooperation.
The meeting between the Indian and Japanese defense ministers – their third in the last four months — also focused on enhancing military and arms industry cooperation between the two countries.
They agreed to accelerate negotiations toward finalizing their first-ever defense technology cooperation initiative under which India and Japan are jointly developing and manufacturing advanced integrated communication antenna systems for Indian Navy warships.
Developed for the Japanese navy, the Unified Complex Radio Antenna (UNICORN) system helps reduce the radar signature of naval vessels. Under the proposed agreement, a state run Indian company will collaborate with Japanese defense firms to co-produce the advanced mast for future Indian navy warships.
New Delhi has been seeking greater Japanese involvement in its defense industry and access to advanced technology as part of its efforts to strengthen domestic manufacturing.
After the talks in Tokyo, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said potential areas for collaboration between the two countries include naval shipbuilding, unmanned and autonomous systems and advanced defense technologies.
Amid their deepening defense cooperation, Japan deployed its fighter jets in India for the first time in September during a bilateral air exercise held in the Indian city of Jodhpur. Tokyo sent F-2A fighter aircraft for the exercise, known as Veer Guardian 2026.
At the recent meeting, both sides agreed to incorporate unmanned systems and increase the complexity of future exercises.

articles.title: Buried in Italy’s budget, officials see Rome meeting NATO spending target
articles.snippet: The numbers cannot be found in this year’s Italian defense budget, but the country has achieved a promised spending total on defense and domestic security equal to 2.8% of GDP in 2026, officials have claimed.
articles.full_text:
ROME — The numbers cannot be found in this year’s Italian defense budget, but the country has achieved a promised spending total on defense and domestic security equal to 2.8% of GDP in 2026, officials have claimed.
That means Italy has fulfilled a promise made at the July NATO summit to hit the 2.8% target as Rome tries to reach the alliance’s 5% objective by 2035, under pressure from U.S. President Trump.
The 5% ambition set down by NATO is split between 3.5% on core defense spending and 1.5% on domestic security spending. Italian officials told Defense News Rome’s spending in the first category hit 2.1% in 2026 and 0.7% in the second category this year, combining for the 2.8% total.
Italy’s 2026 budget, which was issued months late last week, does not clearly state this, and overall patience is required to understand what Italy is spending on each category.
Analysis of the budget starts with pure defense spending, meaning investment, personnel and maintenance and operations cash for the Italian Army, Air Force and Navy, listed as “Funzione Difesa.”
Unlike in previous years, no number is given, but it can be extrapolated from other figures, giving €23.6 billion ($25.8 billion), up from €22.49 billion last year, a €1.1 billion jump.
Within that spend is the key cash for investment or procurement, which is also not specified but can be calculated, by referring to other figures, as €9.33 billion out of the defense ministry’s coffers.
Add in top-funding from Italy’s Enterprise ministry for procurement and the total rises over €12 billion according to a graph which corresponds to the €12.77 billion reached by totaling the amounts listed for each procurement program.
The next total listed is the “Ordinary” defense budget, which adds in domestic spending on Italy’s paramilitary Carabinieri police and other smaller expenses.
That total stands at €32.4 billion in 2026, up 3.6 percent on last year’s €31.3 billion, with spending predicted to rise next year to €32.7 billion.
The next item is the “Integrated” defense budget, which adds all Enterprise Ministry spending, funding from Italy’s finance ministry for overseas military missions and cash from the European Union used for cyber defense.
That total is €36.79 billion, up from €35.49 billion last year.
The complicated calculation does not end there. Next up is the “NATO” budget, which adds in other spending which NATO counts as defense spending.
In the document, the extras are listed as, “Pension spending” and “Spending by other ministries that contribute to national defense.”
The new total is €48.31 billion, which is equal to 2.1% of GDP, up from 2% in 2025.
What the document does not reveal is the domestic security spending Italy then adds on top of that to reach its total figure of 2.8 percent of GDP, as declared at the NATO summit.
Government sources said the remaining cash, equivalent to 0.7% of GDP, is handled outside the defense budget.
Defense News calculated the spending is equal to about €16.1 billion.
The sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity said the spending covers various activities including: frontier control, combatting terrorism, protecting energy infrastructure and crisis preparation.

articles.title: Czech jet engine maker eyes growing role as US supplier in drones, missiles
articles.snippet: Czech jet engine producer PBS Aerospace aims to expand its manufacturing capacity in the United States, targeting at least a twofold increase in its production capacity there.
articles.full_text:
WARSAW, Poland — Czech jet engine producer PBS Aerospace aims to expand its manufacturing capacity in the United States, targeting at least a twofold increase in its production capacity there, according to senior company representatives.
Jan Havránek, PBS Aerospace’s chief government relations and strategy officer, told Defense News that is because the business is booming due to a rising demand for compact propulsion systems used in drones and cruise missiles.
“Everybody wants to build drones and missiles that are fast, fly far, and they want to have them now. That puts scale and quality at the center of the conversation,” Havránek said. “Global conflicts, including the war in Ukraine, have made clear how important it is for the United States to have a reliable domestic supply of these engines, and the market is moving quickly.”
While continuing to produce engines at its factory in Velká Bíteš, in the Czech Republic, PBS Aerospace expanded its American presence in September 2025 with the launch of a plant in Roswell, Georgia. The manufacturing facility was opened as part of a $20 million investment.
“We’re building engines in America, for America,” Havránek said. “Our Georgia facility serves the U.S. market first and foremost, with the U.S. government as our end customer. We supply engines to prime contractors that deliver systems to the Department of War, and we’re proud to help strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base and bring critical manufacturing back onshore.”
In the U.S., the group’s partners include Lockheed Martin and Pratt & Whitney.
To meet rising demand, PBS Aerospace plans to increase its Roswell facility’s annual output to between 10,000 and 20,000 engines over the next three years.
“For next year, we’re looking at up to 5,000 engines to be produced in America,” he said.
With the manufacturing ramp-up in mind, PBS Aerospace is planning to allocate around $100 million to boost its capacity in Roswell, according to Havránek.
Some of the company’s most sought-after products include the TJ40-G1, a compact jet engine that weighs 3.4 kg (7.5 pounds) and delivers up to 425 N of thrust, as indicated by data from the manufacturer.

articles.title: Ford in talks with the Pentagon to supply military vehicles
articles.snippet: Ford said on Tuesday it has held talks with the Pentagon about supplying military vehicles and other defense products to the U.S. military.
articles.full_text:
Ford said on Tuesday it has held talks with the Pentagon about supplying military vehicles and other defense products to the U.S. military, as legacy automakers seek a share of fast-rising defense spending amid tough competition in the auto sector.
A Ford spokesperson said the discussions were focused on supplying highly capable military vehicles and working with U.S.-based space systems contractor Revolution Space to build advanced satellites. Ford had announced on Monday a minority investment in Revolution Space.
The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier in the day that the Pentagon was in talks with General Motors, Ford and other manufacturers to help mass-produce military drones by supplying parts including actuators, engines, sensors and lidar to drone companies.
“The Department of War is actively partnering with domestic manufacturers, suppliers, and emerging tech firms to build a resilient, high-capacity industrial base that accelerates the production, deployment, and long-term sustainment of next-generation unmanned and autonomous systems,” a Pentagon official told Reuters.
Detroit’s automakers have a long history of turning mass production capabilities toward military needs, having converted factories during World War II to build tanks, jet engines and trucks.
According to the Journal’s report, GM is weighing whether to manufacture drone motors, while U.S. defense officials have met with executives at Canadian auto parts maker Magna International and other manufacturing firms, some outside the auto industry.
GM has been most interested in getting involved with military projects at the request of high-ranking defense officials, the Journal said, adding that the automaker was in talks with RTX and L3Harris on a similar deal.
GM declined to comment on the report, but said in an emailed statement that its Defense unit has extensive capabilities and scale, and that it has “demonstrated our commitment to reinforce the U.S. defense-industrial base and help address critical needs.”
Magna said it had nothing to add with regard to the report.
