articles.title: First Dark Eagle hypersonic battery ‘fully fielded,’ Lozano says
articles.snippet: Though the three-star would not share when the first battery was fully fielded, the news comes after the program has faced years of delays.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army has officially fielded its first Long Range Hypersonic Weapon battery, according to the service’s top general in charge of munitions.
“It is fully fielded. It is ready to go,” Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, Program Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Fires, told Breaking Defense on Nov. 19 during an interview. “It is a global deployable and employable warfighting capability. Those soldiers and those units have everything that they need to employ, fight and win.”
Lozano declined to disclose when or where the first battery was fielded, offering few details about the milestone beyond confirming that the weapon is operational and ready for deployment.
The news comes after years of challenges with developing and fielding the LHRW, also known as the Dark Eagle. The Army initially planned to field the first battery in 2023, but testing woes — including a mechanical engineering problem with the launcher — prevented the service from meeting that goal. The Army later pushed its fielding target to September 2025, but missed that deadline as well.
According to a recent report from Bloomberg, the Army had still not completely fielded its first LRHW battery as of October 2026 — putting the service nearly three years behind schedule. The Army’s program office reportedly said in a statement to Bloomberg at the time that it “continues fielding activities” for the Dark Eagle and must undergo more training and other sustainment and readiness work “before declaring the system fully fielded.”
When asked if the report from October was inaccurate, Lozano said he didn’t “want to go so far as to say that.” Instead, he said “this is a rapidly evolving space, and things can happen very quickly, and for all the right reasons, we in the Army and we at PAE [Program Acquisition Executive] Fires are being very, very aggressive about producing, developing and fielding new capabilities that include Dark Eagle.”
Asked when the first battery officially reached full fielding status, Lozano pointed to the fact that some of the weapon’s ground support equipment had been delivered as early as 2021, making it difficult to identify a specific date for the milestone.
Hypersonic Capabilities
Hypersonic missiles can fly at speeds of Mach 5 or greater and are designed to maneuver unpredictably through the Earth’s atmosphere. Over the past several years, both the Pentagon and Congress have shown a growing interest in developing and acquiring such systems, especially as reports have circulated that Russia and China have a number of hypersonic weapons programs in their arsenals.
The Army’s Dark Eagle program was developed alongside the Navy’s Conventional Prompt Strike project. The weapons have the same glide body system, but the Army will integrate it onto ground launchers. The Navy will launch theirs from Zumwalt-class destroyers and Virginia-class submarines once fielded.
One Dark Eagle consists of four trailer-mounted transporter erector launchers, each carrying two all-up rounds plus canisters, along with a battery operations center and support vehicle.
The Army and Navy chose to pause production while addressing problems identified during testing, according to a Government Accountability Office report from July. Further, the GAO report found that “the contractor [Lockheed Martin] has continued to experience issues at its facility.” This has resulted in “missing, inconsistent, and unclear work standards for missile production.”
Lozano declined to provide further details about manufacturing issues, but said preventing similar problems in the future would require more rigorous qualification testing of individual missile components.
That includes “making sure we test all the solid rocket motors, so that we have a high level of confidence that those things work and perform as required, making sure we’re testing and checking out the integrated guidance sections, making sure we’re testing out and qualifying the inertial [navigation] units [and] making sure we’re testing seeker and seeker components,” he said.
Though Lozano declined to comment on where the battery was fielded, Breaking Defense previously reported that soldiers within the 1st Multi-Domain Task Force long-range fires battalion, 5th Battalion, 3rd Field Artillery Regiment at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington received system components and training in anticipation of becoming that first operational unit with the new weapon in 2023.
The Army is now working to field the second and third batteries, though Lozano could not speculate when they would be ready due to operational security concerns. The service is “already over halfway through production” of the third battery, he noted.
“I don’t have a firm date on the wall, I think we’ll see that the second battery and the third battery will realize their full capability at a faster pace and a faster rate than the first battery did,” he said.
New Companies Incoming?
Separately, Lozano indicated the Army could eventually open the LRHW program to additional vendors, potentially introducing more competition that could offer better performing capabilities at a lower cost.
“I’d like to have two or three vendors all in production against a singular requirement, because then that gives me a lot of production flexibility and options,” he said. “Should any one vendor have any kind of quality or production or manufacturing challenge in delivering, it gives me options to kind of maybe buy more or less from one of the vendors over another.”
Lozano said the Army is also pursuing hypersonic weapons that would fill the capability gap between Dark Eagle and shorter-range systems like Castelion’s Blackbeard hypersonic missile through the “scaled hypersonics program.”
The Dark Eagle uses a land-based truck system to fire rounds capable of traveling over 3,800 miles per hour towards targets within a 1,725-mile range. The Blackbeard has a shorter range, smaller form factor and is cheaper. Therefore, platforms discovered through the scaled hypersonics program would ideally have a range between the Blackbeard and Dark Eagle.
“All of our long-range fires efforts and capabilities are significantly important to the Army and to the Department of [Defense], and so they all remain a very high priority for us,” Lozano said.

articles.title: Florida ransomware recovery CEO indicted for allegedly paying hacker ransoms
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The CEO of a ransomware recovery firm was indicted by a federal grand jury over allegations he lied about his services and paid out ransoms to cybercriminals.
articles.full_text:
Florida ransomware recovery CEO indicted for allegedly paying hacker ransoms
The CEO of a ransomware recovery firm was indicted by a federal grand jury after prosecutors accused him of lying about his services and simply paying out ransoms to cybercriminals.
Colombian national Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, is the co-founder of a company based in Florida that marketed itself as a data recovery service for ransomware victims.
Palacio claimed he had decryption tools that allowed him to help victims without negotiating or paying ransomware gangs. Instead, Palacio allegedly paid ransoms and charged his customers enough to make a profit.
Federal agencies have increasingly sought to crack down on the murky industry of ransomware recovery and cybercriminal mediation in recent months.
“As alleged, the defendant preyed on ransomware victims by falsely marketing a solution he did not possess, secretly negotiating with cybercriminals, and profiting from the difference,” said Charles Calenda, first assistant U.S. attorney.
“Businesses and individuals seeking to recover from a cyberattack should not be victimized for a second time by those they turn to for help.”
He is facing three counts of wire fraud, which carry a maximum sentence of 60 years in prison.
Before the DOJ announced the charges, the news outlet 404 Media and independent journalist Brian Krebs published details of Escobar’s operation, writing that he ran a company called Ransomwarehelp.com. The company’s website currently says it is under maintenance.
On Wednesday, Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva confirmed previous reports that the FBI staged an operation in June where they posed as a ransomware gang and victim.
The FBI went to Palacio for assistance and was told his company “never negotiated with or paid the ransom to ransomware attackers but instead could recover the data through its sophisticated decryption technology.”
“The indictment alleges that despite these representations, Palacio did negotiate with and make a payment in the amount of approximately $6,000 in Bitcoin to the purported ransomware actor, which was also an undercover FBI operative, in exchange for the decryption key,” prosecutors said.
“Palacio charged the undercover company approximately $13,260 for his company’s purported decryption technology services.”
He was arrested in Las Vegas on October 22 before being transferred to Rhode Island. He was released on pretrial bond on November 20.
“As alleged, Mr. Palacio Escobar is the proverbial wolf in sheep’s clothing, representing both himself and his company as experts in data recovery, when all the while he was paying the perpetrators of these ransomware attacks, under the guise of helping his clients,” FBI agent Ted Docks said. “Little did they know he was ripping them off.”
A cybersecurity firm that spoke to Krebs claimed it was hired by a ransomware victim who alleged Palacio had deleted the ransomware notes from its system so that he would be the sole person in charge of communicating with the hackers.
Last month, the DOJ charged another Florida-based owner of a ransomware recovery firm for conducting a similar scheme.
Two ransomware negotiators were given four-year sentences in May after pleading guilty to conducting their own covert ransomware attacks and coordinating with ransomware gangs while purportedly negotiating ransoms on behalf of at least five victims.
Another cybersecurity executive was recently arrested and indicted for allegedly being involved in a prominent cybercriminal group that hacked the FBI.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Australia passes tough legislation requiring big tech to preempt foreseeable harms
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The Digital Duty of Care Act sailed through Australia's Parliament. It will mandate that online providers establish protocols to protect users from threats of violence and rape as well as behavior that could cause significant harms.
articles.full_text:
Australia passes tough legislation requiring big tech to preempt foreseeable harms
Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday greenlit legislation creating sweeping online safety reforms that open the possibility of billions of dollars in fines for big tech companies that fail to preempt online harms before they occur.
Known as the Digital Duty of Care Act, the legislation sailed through Parliament with strong backing from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
His administration has been a global leader in fighting against online safety harms and spearheaded Australia’s pioneering strict age requirements for social media use that took effect in December 2025 and have since been copied by governments worldwide.
The pending law will mandate that online providers establish protocols to ensure Australians are protected from threats of violence and rape as well as behavior that could cause significant harms.
Platforms are required to detect and decrease risks from harmful content and must bolster protections for users under 18 against pornography, suicide and eating disorders. They also must undertake annual written risk assessments and call out major platform design changes such as endless scrolling that create new harms.
Under the law, users also will be able to opt out of algorithmic feeds and will be required to prove their age to access porn.
After the law passed, Albanese reportedly told Parliament it will be a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”
“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.”
Similar legislation is already in place in the U.K. and European Union. A bill seeking to impose a duty of care against large platforms has been introduced by U.S. lawmakers but has stagnated in Congress.
U.S. officials have accused the Australian legislation of violating free speech, threatening American companies’ business models and imposing vague requirements that will cause tech giants to overhaul their services to avoid liability.
“We are particularly concerned by potential mandates that would allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements – such as forced chronological feeds or opt-in recommendation systems,” the U.S. Embassies and Consulates in Australia said in a September public comment.
The legislation does not undermine free speech, Albanese told Parliament in October, saying that “rather than someone in the United States deciding” what people see, now Australians can “decide themselves.”
The law will require platforms to “give us more choice over the content and the features that we use, including the feeds that we choose,” Albanese said.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Suspected ransomware attack disrupts cancer treatments, surgeries at Guadeloupe hospital
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: France’s national cybersecurity agency is investigating a suspected ransomware attack that impaired the computer systems of the University Hospital of Guadeloupe, forcing doctors to postpone surgeries, suspend some cancer treatments and revert to pen and paper.
articles.full_text:
Suspected ransomware attack disrupts cancer treatments, surgeries at Guadeloupe hospital
France’s national cybersecurity agency is investigating a suspected ransomware attack that impaired the computer systems of the University Hospital of Guadeloupe, forcing doctors to postpone surgeries, suspend some cancer treatments and revert to pen and paper.
France’s national cybersecurity agency, known as ANSSI, said Tuesday the incident appeared to involve ransomware and that investigators were examining whether hackers gained access to the hospital’s systems through an unnamed IT supplier that was reportedly compromised several months ago.
French prosecutors have launched a criminal investigation into the incident. It remains unclear who was behind the attack. The hospital’s management told local media on Monday that it had not received a ransom demand and ruled out paying a ransom.
The hospital — the largest on the French Caribbean island of approximately 380,000 residents — said on its website it had canceled some surgical procedures, medical consultations and imaging tests through at least Friday.
Radiation therapy has been temporarily suspended over safety concerns, while chemotherapy sessions scheduled for Monday were canceled. The hospital is reviewing upcoming appointments based on each patient’s medical needs.
Emergency services, dialysis treatments and urgent cardiac procedures remain available. The hospital has asked residents to visit its emergency departments only if they need immediate medical care.
Hospital employees first experienced computer and telephone outages on Saturday evening, according to local media reports. What initially appeared to be a technical malfunction turned out to be a cyberattack that encrypted the hospital’s databases.
“We’re back to pen and paper, relying on couriers who travel from one department to another,” the hospital’s director told local media.
As of Tuesday, healthcare workers were still unable to access patients’ electronic medical records and were manually processing prescriptions and collecting laboratory results, slowing patient care.
The hospital has encouraged patients to bring paper copies of their medical records, prescriptions and previous test results to appointments.
It remains unclear whether the hackers stole any personal or medical information. The hospital said it would notify anyone whose data was compromised and warned patients to watch out for phishing attempts by criminals posing as hospital staff.
The hospital plans to gradually restore the affected systems after checking them for malware. Recovery is expected to take several days, but it remains unclear when normal operations will fully resume.
The attack came as the hospital was relocating its operations to a new facility in Belle-Plaine. The French government financed the construction of the new hospital after a major fire damaged its previous facilities in 2017.
According to hospital management, the new facility’s computer systems have stronger security protections, making the disruption easier to manage there. Despite the attack, the hospital has maintained its plans to transfer pediatric emergency services to the new site.
Healthcare under attack
Two other French healthcare organizations — Bordeaux University Hospital and France’s National Cancer Institute — disclosed cyberattacks earlier this week.
Bordeaux University Hospital said it discovered its computer systems had been compromised after detecting that two of its email accounts had been used to send mass emails to employees.
A threat actor known as Scarlettgroup claimed responsibility for the breach, threatening to publish allegedly stolen medical records, prescriptions, laboratory results and financial documents.
The hospital has not confirmed the hackers’ claims and is investigating whether any information was stolen. It temporarily restricted external access to one of its servers as a precaution but said the incident had not disrupted patient care.
France’s National Cancer Institute confirmed Monday that a cyberattack had compromised personal information and disrupted two of its websites. The institute said it had stopped the intrusion but has not disclosed how many people were affected or what information was exposed.
It remains unclear whether the three incidents are linked.
French Health Minister Stephanie Rist said Tuesday the government was working to improve cybersecurity across the country’s healthcare sector and planned to secure long-term funding for these efforts through France’s proposed 2027 social security budget.
“The cybersecurity of our hospitals is also the safety of our patients,” Rist added.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Treasury's FinCEN takes systems offline after cybersecurity incident
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The Treasury Department has taken some systems offline after a cybersecurity incident that “resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.”
articles.full_text:
Treasury's FinCEN takes systems offline after cybersecurity incident
The Treasury Department has taken some systems offline after a cyberattack, according to a notice posted Tuesday evening.
The department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network — commonly known as FinCEN — is “investigating a cybersecurity incident,” the notice posted at the top of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) E-Filing System website said.
The incident “resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems,” according to the banner.
“As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline. The BSA E-Filing website remains operational; however, some services may be temporarily unavailable,” the agency said.
“FinCEN is working diligently to return all systems to normal operations as soon as possible.”
The incident was first reported by The Verge. FinCEN said it is extending deadlines for filers affected by the outages. It urged financial institutions to call a hotline if they need to send suspicious activity reports to law enforcement.
A spokesperson for FinCEN said the FBI and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency are involved in the investigation. Investigators currently believe there is no evidence of any breach of the Bank Secrecy Act or beneficial ownership databases.
No hackers have taken credit for the attack, but several Chinese state-backed groups were accused of breaching the Treasury Department multiple times in 2024 and 2025.
Twelve Chinese nationals, including two officers with China’s Ministry of Public Security (MPS), were charged for the 2024 Treasury breach — which caused outrage across the federal government because the hackers accessed computers used by then-Secretary Janet Yellen and then-Deputy Secretary Adewale Adeyemo.
The FinCEN incident capped a whirlwind Tuesday in which the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and at least two other spy agencies reportedly suffered their own breaches that exposed unclassified information.
The New York Times and NextGov reported that the hackers involved in the CIA breaches allegedly used Artex, a Chinese-made platform that can take any large language model and automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions.
The cyberattacks emerged just days after the FBI said it is investigating its own breach revolving around a critical fugitive database used by U.S. law enforcement agencies.
U.S. federal agencies have been battered by hackers this year. The departments of Defense, Transportation, Justice and Agriculture have all dealt with outages or data breaches caused by cyberattacks. The federal bankruptcy courts were impacted by another cyberattack last month.

articles.title: Colorado says cyberattack took down myColorado app, warns 150,000 had data stolen
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Cybercriminals likely stole data from 150,000 users of myColorado, which residents typically use for digital identification, document storage and accessing state government services.
articles.full_text:
Colorado says cyberattack took down myColorado app, warns 150,000 had data stolen
A critical app used by thousands of Colorado residents for state services was taken down by a cyberattack last week.
The Governor’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) said the incident was discovered on the evening of November 18 and involved hackers breaching the myColorado app — which Colorado residents use for digital identification, document storage and accessing state government services.
OIT shut down the app and began an investigation. The app is still unavailable as of Tuesday afternoon.
The state noted that the app has 2.1 million users and the cyberattack likely involved the theft of data tied to nearly 150,000 people. Investigators declined to provide more information about what data may have been stolen by the cybercriminals.
“We know how much Coloradans rely on these services, and we understand how this is frustrating and inconvenient. Protecting our users’ data is our first priority, and we will bring systems back online as quickly as we can once security is restored,” said Sarah Tuneberg, executive director of OIT.
Colorado urged residents to bring their physical IDs if they are traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Those seeking to access state services can still do so through Colorado agency websites.
The state previously dealt with major cyberattacks on the Department of Higher Education and ransomware attacks on several smaller municipalities.
Several city and state governments are currently dealing with ransomware attacks and cyber incidents, including agencies in New York, Mississippi and California. On Friday, West Virginia’s legislature was knocked offline due to a cyberattack.
Queens Public Library in New York City confirmed it has nearly recovered from a ransomware attack two weeks ago that shut down services at its 66 branches. The library, which serves the borough’s more than 2 million residents, has been forced to operate without digital services.
The attack was claimed on Sunday by The Gentlemen ransomware gang — a cybercriminal group that claimed 398 attacks last quarter. The group far surpassed all other ransomware gangs with the amount of claimed victims, according to researchers at Halcyon.
In Mississippi, Lauderdale County’s more than 70,000 residents were also impacted by a cyberattack on the sheriff’s office on Monday.
The law enforcement agency said it was forced to take its systems offline after the cyberattack. Several services, including the inmate roster listing, are no longer available to the public.

articles.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
articles.snippet: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
articles.full_text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”
Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.
“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”
The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.
“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”
Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.
“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”
The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.
Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.snippet: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
articles.full_text:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.
Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”
Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”
“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”
Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.
One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.
Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.
“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”
Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.
“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”
How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.
“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”
Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.
Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

The operational discipline angle is what stands out – attackers versioning and measuring payloads like product features means defenders need the same rigor about what their third-party tags are allowed to change. Supply-chain reviews for marketing stacks rarely get the scrutiny payments or auth integrations do; this will change that.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.snippet: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.
The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.
The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.snippet: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.
This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.
According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.
Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.
“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”
Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.
Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.
Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”
Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. IT auditors ignored “low risk” flaws reasoning that it took too much effort on the part of attackers to manually exploit them, and that intrusion detection systems would alert them in time to evict human intruders (“hackers”). articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.
Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.
What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.
The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.
